newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House Ethics panel set to meet on Gingrich.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House Ethics panel set to meet on Gingrich.

text.p: The House Ethics Committee was set on Friday to finally discuss the report of a special counsel on House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich that reportedly recommends a reprimand, hefty fine and possible Justice Department probe.

Following days of partisan wrangling, the committee was expected to convene behind closed doors in the morning to review the report by special counsel James Cole, who on Thursday night completed his year-long investigation into ethics charges against Gingrich.
The New York Times and the Baltimore Sun reported Cole's recommendations on Friday, with the Sun saying the fine could be more than $100,000.
Gingrich returned from his home state of Georgia on Thursday, heading into the political maelstrom of the last stage of an investigation into ethics charges against him.
Asked about the investigation as he arrived at the Capitol, Gingrich said: "We're going to do whatever we're asked to do and we're going to try to be helpful."

Democrats have railed against a deadline of next Tuesday for a House vote on the punishment to be meted out to Gingrich for his admitted ethics violations. He is widely expected to be given a reprimand, which would not force him to step down as speaker.
Democratic Caucus chairman Vic Fazio kept up the criticism early Friday.

"They (Republicans) seem to be going through an effort to water it down ... They are attempting to delete things from Mr. Cole's report," he said. "The speaker has a very serious problem," he told CNN.

Gingrich, the first Republican re-elected as speaker in 68 years, admitted "with great sadness" on Dec. 21 that he had provided to investigators "in my name and over my signature, inaccurate, incomplete and unreliable statements." He said he had not intended to mislead the committee.

He also acknowledged he had failed to seek legal advice on whether his use of tax-exempt charitable funds for a college course he taught would violate tax laws. The subcommittee did not take a position on whether the law had been broken.
The ethics committee has been battered by controversy.

First its Republican Chairwoman Nancy Johnson of Connecticut cancelled a week of public hearings. Then the committee's top Democrat, Jim McDermott of Washington state, was forced to step aside following disclosure that he had received a tape of an illegally monitored telephone conversation between Gingrich and top aides that was later leaked to the press.

Partisan quarreling over the two developments soured the opening of a new Congress which was supposed to have set a tone of cooperation and bipartisanship at the start of President Bill Clinton's second term.
